the "
Psi Upsilon Epitome
"
will be a work of superior
excellence. Nothwithstanding the value of our cata
logue as an encyclopedia of Fraternity information, we
need a complete and classified history of Psi Upsilon
from its foundation to the present time. Many im
portant facts have fallen out of sight in the confused
mass of memorabilia; but Mr. Jacob's research has
given them order and ably systematized them in
the Epitome.
The "
Chapter Annals
"
give the history of the sev
eral chapters separately, and contain information that
will be interesting and entirely new to those even
who are well versed in Fraternity affairs. In this field
there is a great temptation to treat subjects that cannot
properly be discussed in public ; but, we are
pleased
to say, in no particular can the author be charged with
the least violation of secrecy. The "Chronology,"
divided into six decades, is full and accurate, and will
prove invaluable to members and Chapters. Upon the
remainder of the work, we will reserve judgment until
it is published.
The members of the Chi have recently issued a cir
cular letter to their graduates, giving information in
regard to all the important Fraternity events of the
year and also calling attention to the coming Conven
tion. The Chi has been in the habit of from time
to time sending a letter to her Alumni, and the interest
which her graduates take in her welfare is largely at
tributable to that fact. This is a
practice which should
be adopted by every Chapter ; for it keeps the gradu
ate alive to the interests of his Chapter. Such a
circular need not be restricted to Chapter matters,
but may be made very valuable as a means of infor
mation on College as well as Fraternity subjects, and
would be greatly appreciated by the graduate who is,
unfortunately, too often forgotten, except when the
treasury must be replenished.
The usefulness of a Fraternity is largely measurable
by the extent to which the members, active and grad
uate, are bound together. If the bond of interest is
allowed to weaken the graduate's relation of member
ship is, in effect, severed. The position of an Alumnus
is necessarily isolated, and his interest soon dies out
unless he is in some way in communication with his
Chapter. The experience of several Chapters has
proved that they are benefitted by sending all their
graduates invitations to the annual initiation. If a still
further advance should be made upon this system, it
would be attended with much greater advantages.
Annual Conventions and the frequent meetings of
Alumni Associations are every year perfecting a closer
union between the members of the Fraternity, and this
would be greatly supplemented by the adoption of the
method which we advocate. If every Chapter would
follow the plan for two or three years, the advantages
would be patent and it would soon become a recog
nized and estabhshed usage of the Fraternity.
The efforts which several of the brothers are making
to form a New York Alumni association, will evidently
meet with success. A date has been fixed for a grand

54 THE DIAMOND,
banquet, and those who have the matter in hand are
men of energy and ability.
Several of our prominent graduates have given
countenance to the project, and have signified their
intention of being present. If the members are
judicious in their selection of officers, a
prosperous
career will be insured to the association. Every Psi
Upsilon in New York city should support this move
ment and, by his attendance at the meeting, give the
association his aid and encouragement.

PSI UPSILON AT CORNELL.
The graduate representation of Psi Upsilon of Cor
nell is unusually large. Many of the members of the
Faculty are honored representatives of the Fraternity,
and all these hold important positions in their various
departments. In the town, also, are
many prominent
members of Psi Upsilon. In view of these facts it
seems
fitting that mention should be made of these
i members, and such points in the personal history of
each touched upon, as have come to our
knowledge,
and will be of interest to Psi Upsilons in general. It
may not seem out of place also to show the interest
manifested by them in the* affairs of the Cornell Chap
ter and of the Fraternity at large, since it was
through
their untiring efforts that the Chapter came into ex
istence.
The career of Andrew D. White, President of the
University, is one full of interesting details, few of
which can be mentioned here. In 1853 he graduated
from Yale College a leader in his class and a member
of that honored literary society, �P. B. K. In 1855 he
went as attach^ to the United States legation at St.
Petersburg. In 185 7 he accepted the Professorship of
History and English Literature at Michigan University.
From 1863-66 President White held the office of
Senator of the State of New York and Chairman of the
Committee on Education. In 1866 he became Presi
dent of Cornell University, which important position
he now holds. Several times have other duties called
him away for a
longer or shorter period ; as United
States Commissioner to St. Domingo in 1870; as
United States Commissioner to the Paris Exposition
in 1878 and lastly as Minister to Germany firom 187981. The untiring and successful efforts of President
White are shown in the increased prosperity of the
University of which he is the able head. As a Psi
Upsilon one finds in him a
man, who, despite all his
official cares and responsibilities, has a warm feeling
for the welfare of the Fraternity, and takes a deep in
terest in the Chi Chapter of which he was one of the
most zealous founders.
Rev. Charles C. Shackford, Professor of Rhetoric
and General Literature, graduated from Harvard
University in 1835 as valedictorian of his class. In
1838 the degree of A. M. was conferred upon him by
that institution. He has held the position of Professor
in Cornell University since '71. In a literary line
Professor Shackford has contributed many articles for
the North American Review, the Christian Examiner
and Harper's Magazine; and is also known for his
translation of Auerbach's "Villa Eden," 1868, and of
Auerbach's "
German Tales," 1869. Although not
belonging to the Fraternity until initiated at the Chi
Chapter in 1876, he is one of the most enthusiastic
members, and his frequent attendance upon meetings,
and evident enjoyment of them, shows that, though
his hair may be well streaked with gray, he is in spirit
as
young as the youngest among us.
Waterman Thomas Hewett, Professor of German

THE DIAMOND. 55
since 1870, is a
graduate of the class of sixty-nine,
Amherst College. Prof. Hewett's name appears fre
quently in the Chapter Archives during the years of
'75 and '76 when the Chapter was being founded. He
will be remembered as being associate editor for the
Gamma of the Psi U Catalogue for 1878.
Rev. Charles Babcock, dean of the Department of
Architecture since 1871, is a graduate of the Theta,
class of 1847. He is author of a work on
"
Elemen
tary Architecture
"
published in 1876. Although, on
account of ill-health he is not as frequent a visitor as
formerly, he is, nevertheless, a
strong Psi U, ready
and willing to aid us when assistance of any kind is
desired.
Albert Nelson Prentiss, dean of the Botanical De
partment since 1868, and Horatio Stevens White,
Professor in the German Department are, with Pro
fessor Shackford, our most frequent visitors. The
former, like Professor Shackford, was initiated at Cor
nell when the Chapter was founded. He graduated
from the Michigan Agricultural College in 1861, and
held the Professorship of Botany and Horticulture in
that institution from 1863 until he came to Cornell in
1868. Apropos of his department. Professor Prentiss
has written, "My Vineyard at Lake View" (1866),
also the first Walker Prize Essay before the Boston
Society of Natural History,
"
On the Mode of Natural
Distribution of Plants over the Surface of the Earth.
"
Professor White is a
graduate of Harvard, class of '71,
and is one of the last representatives of our
only and
necessarily extinct Chapter.
Hemy Shales Williams, Professor of Geology and
Paleontology, was also initiated here. He is a gradu
ate of Yale Scientific School 1868, from which institu
tion he received the degree of Ph. D. in 1871. The
position which Professor Williams holds in scientific
circles is shown by the honors conferred upon him by
the scientific societies at home and abroad.
Professor Williams is warmly interested in the Society
and Chapter ; more especially because of his having a
brother and cousin at present active members of the
Chapter. This ends the list of Psi U professors now
resident in Ithaca, but the list will hardly seem com
plete until the Psi U professors who have but recently
left the University as well as the present non-resident
professors have been mentioned. Among the former
is one whose relations to the Chi were so close and
intimate, while he was in the University, as to make
his name almost a synonym for that of the Chapter.
Prof. Willard Fiske, formerly dean of the Department
of German and North European languages, and Libra
rian of Cornell University, was a member of the class
of '51, Hamilton College, from which institution he
received the degree of A. M. in 1856. In 1850-51
Professor Fiske went as attach^ to the United States
Legation at Copenhagen. From 1852-9 he held the
position as Assistant Librarian at the Astor Library,
New York City. During his college days and later
Professor Fiske is said to have been a fine chess player
and passionately fond of the game. In 1859 he pub
lished a book on
"
The American Chess Congress."
In an editorial and literary line he has been a contrib
utor to the Stockholm Aftonblad, to the London Notes
and Queries, and in this country, a contributor to the
New York Tribune, Evening Post", Nation, and Liter
ary World. For the Fraternity he has done much in
the way of writing. As founder of the Diamond, 1878,
he has won for himself a
lasting reputation among Psi
Upsilon. Professor Fiske is also distinguished as
associate editor for the Theta of that most complete
work of its kind, the Psi U Catalogue for 1878. The
songs he has written for the Fraternity are numerous
and popular. While at Cornell Professor Fiske was
looked upon as the chief organizer and mainstay of
the Chapter. Nowhere were the boys more sure of an
hospitable welcome and of being well entertained than
at the house of Professor Fiske. But, aside from this
hospitable kindness, the Chapter was remembered by
tokens of a more lasting nature. No matter where he
might be, in France or
Germany, traveling or
busy,
he never for a moment seemed to forget the Chapter or
fail to discover in his travels something that would be
an addition to the Ubrary or an ornament to the rooms.
Wm. Edward Lucas, Professor of Rhetoric, left us
but a year ago to accept the position of private secre
tary to the Mayor of New York City. He graduated
from Cornell in '77 and seemed as much a
companion
as professor ; and there was no one to whom we were
more ready to go, or who was more willing to assist us
in time of trouble. His successor in the department of
Rhetoric, Wm. H. Carpenter, left at the close of last
year to accept an Assistant Professorship in German
at Columbia College, having been here but two terms.
He was as Professor Lucas, a
graduate of Cornell,
and like him seemed one of the Chapter. His depart
ure was a source of regret to us all.
Among the non-resident professors we have some
of the most distinguished names on the long list of
non-residents. Goldwin Smith, whose lectures on
English History are so deservedly popular, was initiated
at the time our Chapter was established. He gradu
ated from the University of Oxford in 1845, ^"^^ '^^o

56 THE DIAMOND.
years later received the degree of A. M. from that
institution. His reputation as a scholar both in Eng
land and this country, is such that further mention
seems hardly necessary. From 1858-66 he held the
position of Regus Professor of Modern History in the
University of Oxford. He . has been contributor to
the "Encyclopedia Britannica" (8th edition), to the
North British Review, the Contetnporary Review, the
North American Review, the London Daily News,
and numerous other periodicals. Charles Kendall
Adams is professor of History at Michigan University,
and a graduate of the class of '61. He has held the
position of professor in that institution since 1867.
His lectures are instructive and popular, and he takes
high rank among the historians of this country. The
great work, which first won him the high reputation he
now holds, is his
"
Democracy and Monarchy
"
in
France. His most recent work is a Manual of English
History, the third edition of which is now in the pubhsher's hands. His lectures are
by no means dry, but
often replete with wit and humor. Socially Professor
Adams is a
very pleasant man to meet, and exceed
ingly entertaining. He shows much interest in the
affairs of Psi Upsilon and especially in the matters of
the Phi Chapter. He was initiated into the Fraternity
in 1865, when the Phi Chapter was founded.
Another non-resident professor, whose name has
recently been added to the list, is Charles Dudley
Warner, who is to deliver a course of lectures on
Modern Literature in the Spring term. As is well
known from the excellent article which appeared in
the last Diamond, Mr. Warner is a
graduate of Hamil
ton. He and Professor Fiske were members of the
same class and fast friends while in College. His
reputation as an author is so well established as to
make him readily known by all American readers.
His
"
Back Log Studies
"
and "
Being a Boy
"
possess a
freshness and originality which makes them attractive
to all classes of readers.

THE CONVENTION.
Preparations for the Fifty-first Annual Convention
are drawing to a close, and, although there will doubt
less be some changes and additional features intro
duced later, the general programme of events will be as
herein stated. Each day brings news of prominent
Psi U's and large Chapter delegations who expect to
be present. It is confidently expected that between
one hundred and fifty and two hundred members of
the Fraternity will be in attendance. Especially wel
come is the news that the extreme Eastern and West
ern Chapters will be largely represented. These, with
the unusually large number of undergraduates who are
coming from the Theta, the Psi, the Pi, the Upsilon,
and the Eta, will make the Convention remarkable for
the attendance of active members. Such an assem
blage cannot but give a powerful impulse to Fraternity
work, and be the means of arousing renewed enthusi
asm among our graduate brethren.
The days of the Convention are Wednesday and
Thursday, May 7th and '8th. The business session
will commence on
Wednesday morning, at 10.30

THE DIAMOND. 57
o'clock, and extend through both days. The com
mittee have been especially fortunate in securing for
this purpose the Masonic rooms, in the Masonic block,
on Tioga street. Nothing could be better suited to
the needs of the Fraternity. The rooms are elegantly
furnished, perfectly secluded, supplied with every con
venience, and within one minute's walk of all the
prominent hotels. On Wednesday evening at eight
o'clock will occur
THE RECEPTION,
in the University gymnasium and armory. Hitherto
it has been customary at conventions to hold both the
Hterary. exercises and reception on the same
evening.
Under this rule the reception was never fairly com
menced before eleven o'clock, the guests had to be
transported from one hall to another, and few felt like
dancing after Hstening to orations and essays for two or
three consecutive hours. To obviate these objections
the entire evening will this year be devoted to the re
ception. The hall is very large, easily accommodating
five hundred people, will be lighted by electricity, and
gaily decorated with society emblems, Cornell boating
trophies, etc. The music will be furnished by the 54th
Regiment band, of Rochester. One feature of the
order of dances will be a Psi U waltz and landers,
composed by Bro. G. B. Penny, of the Chi. These
will not only be a novelty, but a valuable addition to
the Hst of Fraternity music. Ladies are coming to at
tend the reception from Syracuse, Binghamton, El
mira, Rochester, Auburn, and other places in Central
New York. Teall, of Rochester, will act as caterer.
THE LAYING OE THE CORNER-STONE.
The corner-stone of the new Chi Chapter-house wiU
be laid either on Wednesday or Thursday afternoon at
half-past four o'clock. Circumstances make it impos
sible to fix the exact day. The ceremonies will con
sist of speeches by Charles Dudley Warner and other
eminent brethren, and songs by the Fraternity. Be
fore these exercises are over the entire scene will be
photographed.
THE PUBLIC literary EXERCISES.
On Thursday evening, at eight o'clock, in Wilgus
Opera House, will occur the public literary exercises.
These will be presided over by Hon. Sterling G. Had
ley, of Waterloo, N. Y., one of the founders of the
Fraternity. Prof. W. W. Goodwin, J., '51, of Har
vard College, will deliver an address. His subject will
be his recent work in Greece, as Director of the Amer
ican School at Athens. A rich treat, we are sure, is
in store for those who will hear Professor Goodwin.
Prof A. S. Hardy, F, '68, of Dartmouth College, wellknown as the author of several text-books upon the
higher mathematics, and still better known, perhaps, as
the author of the recent novel "But Yet a Woman,"
will read the poem. Prof. Goodwin Smith, X., '46,
will read the essay. An interesting feature of the pro
gramme, and one which the whole Fraternity will hail
with dehght, will be a short poem by Hon. Francis M.
Finch, Judge of the Court of Appeals, in which he will
explain why he could not write the Convention Ode.
Even though the Fraternity loses another song by this
well-known Psi Upsilon lyrist, we feel sure that She will
gain more by his explanatory poem. Rev. T. T.
Munger, D.D., B., '51, will act as Chaplain. Frater
nity songs will be interspersed throughout the exer
cises.
THE convention BANQUET.
Immediately after the public exercises, the brethren
will adjourn to Library Hall for the banquet. Judge
Albion W. Tourgee, F., '62, will preside, and responses
to toasts are expected from Hon. Sterling G. Hadley,
0., '36, President Andrew D. White, B., '53, Prof.
James M. Pierce, A., '55, Charles Dudley Warner, W.,
'51, Rev. Joseph H. Twichell, D.D., B., '65, George
W. Elliott, H, '73, Herbert L. Bridgman, F., '66, and
many others. It is absolutely necessary to the com
plete success of the banquet that the committee of
arrangements be informed of the number of those who
expect to be present. Therefore each Chapter and
every individual Psi U is requested to send, before
May ist, to S. B. Turner, Esq., Ithaca, N. Y., the
names, or at least, the number of the brethren who
are coming. Should circumstances require it, none
.
but those who have complied with this request wiU be
admitted to the banquet. The banquet tickets will be
^4, and may be obtained from the above mentioned
gentleman.
convention HEADQUARTERS.

BOOK REVIEW.
The Expositor in the Pulpit. By Marvin R. Vincent, D.D., New York:
Anson D. F. Randolph & Company.
Among the many valuable religious books which this
publishing house turns out, is a
thoughtful little work,
"The Expositor in the Pulpit," by Rev. Dr. Marvin
R. Vincent, A., '54. The position which its author
occupies in the theological world is, of course, a suffi
cient guarantee of its excellence. The book is de
signed for instruction to those who are in or are
about to take up the ministry, and is written in a
very
attractive style. The teaching is enforced by wellchosen illustrations.

Eugene Schuyler, Beta, '59, is the present MinisterResident and Consul-General at Athens.
Hon. W. B. Ruggles, Psi '49, State Superintendent
of Public Instruction, has accepted an invitation to
deliver the annual oration before the Society of Hamil
ton Alumni, next commencement. The Society draws
on the Psi this year for both orator and poet.
John G. Saxe, Alpha '53, is growing gradually weaker
at his home in Brooklyn. He suffers from cerebro
spinal meningitis, complicated with partial paralysis by
being buried under a railroad train in an accident on
the Pan Handle road, years ago. It is not probable
that the once brilliant man will survive long.
On Wednesday, April 16, were married Miss Emma
Elise Stone, daughter of Mr. M. W. Stone, of New
Brighton, Staten Island, and Mr. Ernest Fitzyale Bir
mingham, Delta, '79, publisher of The American
Queen. The ceremony took place at St. John's Epis
copal church, Clifton, Staten Island, the Rev. Dr.
Cornelius E. Swope, of Trinity chapel, officiating.
Mr. E. P. Whipple [Gamma '50], is not 70 years of
age yet, but he ranks among our older Htterateurs.
He lives quietly, and does much less work than
was formerly his wont. He has completed a
paper on
Matthew Arnold, which is soon to appear. Mrs. Whip
ple gives receptions which have both a
literary and
social character, and gather many of our
younger as
well as older people of note in her T^aiXois.�Hartford

As a
possible candidate for the Presidency, Senator
Joseph R. Hawley, Psi, '4 7, is portrayed in the New
York Tribune :
"
Born in the South, his earliest associa
tions and his latest sympathies are with that suffering
section. Bred in the North, his culture, faith and
political training have had their root in the hardy soil
of New England. Before the Repubhcan party had its
birth he was a
Republican. He preached the Re
publican gospel from every stump and every schoolhouse, when even in Connecticut to be an
anti-slavery

THE DIAMOND. 59
man was to be an Ishmselite. When Lincoln called
for the first 75,000, he was the first soldier who stood
forth on Connecticut soil to show his faith by his
works, and if needs be, by his blood. He fought all
through the war, from the ranks to the epaulettes, and
from Bull Run to the apple-tree at Appomatox. He is
